items.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Michael Woods, Clinton, New York, September 23, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Ever since the Benny Goodman-Chase Manhattan ad, you know.

ctx.x: Tell us about the clarinet, because it’s artists of your ilk that keep this instrument in the forefront.

You think so? Some people might say the opposite. Some people might say we’re helping to bury it. It’s an instrument which could go the way of the oboe d’amour or the viola da gamba. It’s a very difficult instrument. To quote Jerry Dodgion it was invented by two guys who didn’t know each other. There’s no rhyme nor reason for it. You have to be some kind of a sadist, masochist-sadist to continue on this instrument. It’s not the voice of bebop, it’s not the voice of today so to speak, even though there are more…

items.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: you’d see Benny Goodman rehearsing, you’d see Artie Shaw rehearsing

ctx.x: Oh yes. A lot of people have mentioned that.

Yeah. We just used to hang around there looking at — you’d see Benny Goodman rehearsing, you’d see Artie Shaw rehearsing, you’d see Tommy Dorsey rehearsing. And there was Shep Fields rehearsing. Well I said what harm could this do? And there was a sign out there, we need a baritone sax and bass clarinet players, so fine, boom, I sat down in the chair and played. Oh good, what’s your name kid? And that’s how I got with Ralph Flanagan. I finally graduated high school and then they held the auditions, and word got…

Thompson?” He said, “Yes I am.” I said, “My name is Kenny Davern and I can’t wait this line, you see I have a gig” — which I was lying through my teeth — “I have to be at a gig in about 45 minutes and I wonder if it would be possible for me to—” He said, “Okay.” And he took me in. Well there in back of the screen was Ralph Flanagan putzing around on the piano and a bass player and a drummer. And he puts up the sheet music and I take out my horn.
